questions.question: What is the difference between Decorator pattern and subclassing?
questions.title: Decorator vs subclassing
questions.direct_answer: Subclassing adds behavior at compile time and creates a fixed class hierarchy, while Decorator wraps objects at runtime and composes behaviors flexibly without modifying existing classes. Subclassing is inheritance; Decorator is composition.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the composition-over-inheritance principle and can articulate when each is appropriate.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying they're interchangeable or just syntactic choices—they have fundamentally different trade-offs and use cases.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Open/Closed Principle: Decorator lets you extend behavior without modifying the original class, while subclassing requires changing the hierarchy.

sections.title: Subclassing vs Decorator: Fundamental Difference
sections.content:
The core difference is **when and how behavior is added**. **Subclassing** uses inheritance to add behavior at compile time by creating new classes that extend existing ones—the hierarchy is fixed when you write the code. **Decorator** uses composition to wrap objects at runtime, adding behavior by holding a reference to the original object and delegating to it—the wrapping happens when you instantiate objects. Subclassing is for **type specialization**: a Manager is-a specialized Employee with additional responsibilities, and this relationship is permanent.

Decorator is for **optional responsibilities**: an Order can be wrapped with GiftWrapDecorator or ExpressShippingDecorator based on user choices at checkout. Think of subclassing like building a house with rooms designed into the blueprint—the structure is fixed. Decorator is like furniture you add to rooms after construction—you can rearrange, add, or remove pieces without changing the house structure. The **Open/Closed Principle** highlights the difference: Decorator extends behavior without modifying existing classes, while subclassing requires changing the inheritance tree when requirements change.

sections.title: Subclassing vs Decorator at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Subclassing|~Compile-time|inheritance (is-a)|fixed hierarchy|2^N for combos
blue|Decorator|~Runtime|composition (has-a)|wrap and delegate|N+1 for combos
emerald|Open/Closed|~Extend, don't modify|new decorator = new class|original untouched|stack dynamically
violet|Pick by intent|~Type vs responsibility|is-a -> subclass|optional add-on -> decorate|combinable -> decorate

sections.title: Subclassing vs Decorator in Code
Subclassing vs Decorator Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Subclassing | Decorator |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When behavior is added | Compile time (when writing classes) | Runtime (when creating objects) |
| Mechanism | Inheritance (is-a relationship) | Composition (has-a wrapped object) |
| Flexibility | Fixed hierarchy, can't change after compilation | Dynamic wrapping, add/remove at runtime |
| Class count growth | Exponential with optional features | Linear with optional features |
| Modifying original class | Requires changing inheritance tree | No modification, just wrap existing objects |

sections.title: When to Choose Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **subclassing** when you're modeling a stable type hierarchy where subclasses specialize parent behavior: Animal → Mammal → Dog is a natural taxonomy where each subclass refines the concept.

Use it when behavior is **fixed at object creation** and won't change: a SavingsAccount is always a SavingsAccount, never becoming a CheckingAccount.

Use **Decorator** when you have optional, combinable behaviors that can be mixed at runtime: adding validation, logging, caching, or retry logic to services—these can be stacked in any combination based on configuration.

Use it when the **Open/Closed Principle** matters: you want to add features without modifying existing classes, so new decorators extend functionality without touching the original service.

Use Decorator when inheritance would create class explosion: 3 optional features need 8 subclasses but only 4 decorators.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using subclassing for optional features**: Freshers create subclasses like ServiceWithLogging, ServiceWithCaching, ServiceWithLoggingAndCaching—this creates exponential class growth and tight coupling between concerns. Use Decorator for optional features that combine.
- **Using Decorator for type hierarchies**: Wrapping a Car with a VehicleDecorator to turn it into a Truck misses that these are distinct types with different contracts—inheritance is correct for modeling type relationships.
- **Thinking they're syntactically equivalent**: Saying inheritance is just syntax and Decorator is just composition ignores that they have fundamentally different runtime behavior—inheritance is static and Decorator is dynamic.
- **Not considering the Open-Closed Principle**: Using subclassing means adding new behavior requires modifying the class hierarchy, while Decorator lets you add behavior by writing new decorators without touching existing code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Timing difference**: Subclassing adds behavior at compile time when you define classes; Decorator adds behavior at runtime when you wrap objects
- **Inheritance vs composition**: Subclassing uses is-a inheritance relationships; Decorator uses has-a composition by wrapping objects
- **Flexibility**: Subclassing creates fixed hierarchies; Decorator allows dynamic addition and removal of behaviors based on runtime conditions
- **Class explosion**: Subclassing with N optional features needs 2^N classes; Decorator needs N+1 classes, growing linearly instead of exponentially
- **Open/Closed Principle**: Decorator extends behavior without modifying existing classes; subclassing requires changing the inheritance tree when adding features
- **Type specialization**: Subclassing is correct for modeling true type hierarchies (Manager is-an Employee); Decorator is for optional responsibilities
- **Delegation chain**: Decorator wraps objects in layers, each delegating to the next; subclassing overrides methods, calling super where needed

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Subclassing and Decorator solve different problems. Subclassing uses inheritance to add behavior at compile time. You define classes that extend other classes, and the hierarchy is fixed when you write the code. Decorator uses composition to wrap objects at runtime. You hold a reference to another object and delegate to it after adding behavior. Subclassing is for type specialization. A Manager is-an Employee with extra responsibilities—that's a permanent relationship. You use inheritance to model it. Decorator is for optional behaviors. An Order might need gift wrapping or express shipping based on user choices. You wrap the order with decorators at runtime based on what the user selected. The key difference is flexibility. With subclassing, behavior is fixed when you compile. Once you create an ExpressShippingOrder subclass, every instance has express shipping permanently. With Decorator, you wrap at runtime. You can add or remove decorators based on conditions, user preferences, or configuration. Another difference is class count. Say you have three optional features. With subclassing, you need eight classes to cover all combinations: base, feature-A, feature-B, feature-C, A-plus-B, A-plus-C, B-plus-C, A-plus-B-plus-C. With Decorator, you need four classes: base plus three decorators. That's exponential versus linear growth. Subclassing also violates the Open-Closed Principle. When requirements change, you modify the inheritance tree, adding new subclasses. Decorator lets you add behavior by writing new decorators without touching existing code. One mistake freshers make is using subclassing for everything because it's simpler. But when you need combinations of optional features, you end up with a giant inheritance tree that's brittle and hard to extend.

questions.question: How would you use the Decorator pattern to add caching to a repository?
questions.title: Decorator for caching
questions.direct_answer: Create a CachingUserRepository that implements UserRepository, wraps the real repository via constructor injection, checks a cache Map before delegating to the wrapped repository, and stores results in the cache after successful retrieval. This keeps caching logic separate from data access logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can apply Decorator to a real Spring Boot repository layer—not just services or abstract examples.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding cache logic directly inside the repository implementation—couples infrastructure concerns to data access and makes testing harder.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Compare manual Decorator to Spring's at-Cacheable annotation and explain when you'd choose each—manual gives control, at-Cacheable gives convenience.

sections.title: Decorator Pattern for Repository Caching
sections.content:
Applying Decorator to a **Spring Boot repository** involves wrapping the repository with a caching layer that intercepts queries, checks an in-memory cache, and only delegates to the real repository on cache misses. The **CachingUserRepository** implements the same UserRepository interface, holds a reference to the actual repository (like JpaUserRepository), and maintains a **ConcurrentHashMap** as the cache store. On reads like findById, it checks the cache first—if present, return immediately. If absent, delegate to the wrapped repository, store the result, and return. On writes like save or delete, delegate first, then update the cache to keep it consistent. This separates **caching infrastructure** from **data access logic**—the real repository doesn't know it's being cached, and the cache decorator doesn't know about JPA or database specifics.

Think of it like a library checkout system: the cache is the returns desk that checks if a book is already back before sending someone to the stacks (database)—it speeds up common requests without changing how the stacks are organized.

sections.title: Caching Decorator at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|UserRepository|~Shared interface|real + decorator implement it|substitutable|client unaware
blue|CachingUserRepository|~The decorator|wraps real repo|ConcurrentHashMap cache|delegates on miss
emerald|Read path|~Cache-aside|hit -> return|miss -> delegate + store|fast repeat reads
violet|Write path|~Keep consistent|save -> DB then cache|delete -> evict entry|avoid stale data

sections.title: Caching Repository Decorator Implementation
When to Use Repository Caching Decorator
sections.content:
Use manual caching decorator when you need **fine-grained control** over cache behavior: custom eviction policies (remove entries after 5 minutes), conditional caching (only cache users with specific roles), or multi-level caching (in-memory + Redis).

Use it when your cache logic is **complex enough** that annotations can't express it: caching query results with dynamic keys based on multiple parameters, or updating related cache entries when one entity changes.

Use it in **development and testing** to add caching temporarily without modifying production code—swap CachingUserRepository for JpaUserRepository in configuration.

Prefer **Spring's at-Cacheable** annotation for simple cases: it uses dynamic proxies (which are decorators under the hood) and integrates with Spring Cache abstraction, supporting Redis, Caffeine, or other cache providers. Manual decorator makes sense when at-Cacheable's limitations (method-level caching, limited key customization) don't fit your needs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding cache logic inside repository implementation**: Freshers put cache checks directly in JpaUserRepository methods, mixing caching infrastructure with data access code—this violates Single Responsibility and makes the repository harder to test and maintain.
- **Not invalidating cache on writes**: Caching reads but forgetting to update or remove cache entries on save or delete causes stale data—users see old values because the cache isn't synchronized with the database.
- **Using non-thread-safe collections**: Using HashMap instead of ConcurrentHashMap for the cache in multi-threaded environments causes race conditions—concurrent reads and writes can corrupt the map or return inconsistent data.
- **Caching mutable objects without copying**: Storing User objects in cache without defensive copying means clients can modify cached instances, corrupting the cache—either use immutable records or clone objects before caching.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Repository interface**: Decorator implements the same UserRepository interface as the wrapped JPA repository to maintain substitutability
- **ConcurrentHashMap cache**: Use thread-safe map for in-memory caching in multi-threaded Spring Boot apps—HashMap causes race conditions
- **Cache-check-then-delegate**: On reads, check cache first; on miss, delegate to wrapped repository and store result for future requests
- **Write-through cache**: On writes (save, delete), delegate to repository first to persist, then update cache to keep it consistent with database
- **Cache invalidation**: Remove entries from cache on delete operations and update entries on save—stale cache data causes incorrect behavior
- **at-Cacheable comparison**: Spring's annotation uses dynamic proxies (Decorator under the hood) for simple caching—manual decorator gives control for complex scenarios
- **Separation of concerns**: Caching logic lives in decorator, data access logic lives in JPA repository—neither knows about the other's implementation

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To add caching to a repository with Decorator, you create a CachingUserRepository that implements UserRepository, wraps the real repository like JpaUserRepository, and uses a ConcurrentHashMap as the cache. On reads like findById, the decorator checks the cache first. If it's there, return the cached user—that's a cache hit. If not, delegate to the wrapped repository to fetch from the database, store the result in the cache, and return it. On writes like save or delete, you delegate to the wrapped repository first to persist changes, then update the cache. For save, you put the new user in the cache. For delete, you remove the entry. This keeps the cache consistent with the database. The key is that the real repository doesn't know it's being cached. The JpaUserRepository just does JPA queries. The cache logic lives entirely in the decorator. That's separation of concerns—caching infrastructure is separate from data access. One mistake freshers make is putting cache checks directly inside the repository implementation. That couples caching to data access and makes testing harder. Another is using a regular HashMap instead of ConcurrentHashMap—in a multi-threaded Spring Boot app, concurrent reads and writes will corrupt the map or cause exceptions. You need thread safety. A third mistake is not invalidating the cache on writes. If you cache reads but forget to update the cache on save or remove entries on delete, users see stale data. Now, Spring has at-Cacheable annotation that does this automatically using dynamic proxies. That's Decorator under the hood—Spring wraps your repository in a caching proxy at runtime. For simple cases, use the annotation. For complex scenarios where you need custom eviction, conditional caching, or multi-level caches, write a manual decorator.

questions.question: What is the role of the component interface in the Decorator pattern?
questions.title: Decorator component interface role
questions.direct_answer: The component interface is the shared contract that both the concrete component and all decorators implement. It ensures decorators can transparently wrap the real object—clients interact with the interface, not knowing whether they're calling the real component or a stack of decorators.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why Decorator requires an interface to work—not just how to implement the pattern mechanically.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the decorator just extends the concrete class directly—that breaks substitutability and tight-couples decorator to one implementation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect this to the Liskov Substitution Principle—decorators are substitutable for the component because they share the interface, and explain how that enables runtime composition.

sections.title: Component Interface: The Contract That Enables Decoration
sections.content:
The **component interface** is the foundation of the Decorator pattern—it defines the contract that both the concrete component and all decorators must implement. This shared contract enables **transparent wrapping**: clients interact with the interface (e.g., UserRepository or Coffee), and they don't know whether they're calling the real component (JpaUserRepository or SimpleCoffee) or a stack of decorators (CachingUserRepository wrapped in LoggingUserRepository). The interface enforces **substitutability**—decorators can stand in for the real component anywhere in the code because they implement the same methods.

Think of it like electrical outlets: the interface is the socket shape and voltage standard, the concrete component is a lamp plugged in, and decorators are power strips or surge protectors—as long as everything follows the outlet contract, you can stack adapters between the wall and the lamp without the lamp knowing. Without the interface, you'd have to extend the concrete class directly, which tight-couples decorators to one implementation and breaks when you want to wrap different concrete components.

sections.title: Component Interface at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Component interface|~Shared contract|both implement it|PaymentProcessor|key to wrapping
blue|Concrete component|~Real work|Stripe / PayPal|does the actual job|the wrapped target
emerald|Decorator|~Wraps interface type|field is the interface|wraps any impl|delegates + adds
violet|Substitutability|~Liskov in action|decorator stands in|client sees interface|runtime composition

sections.title: Component Interface Enabling Substitutability
Why Interface Type Matters
sections.content:
The component interface type matters when you need **decorator reusability**: one LoggingDecorator works with StripePaymentProcessor, PayPalPaymentProcessor, or any future payment processor because they all implement PaymentProcessor. Without the interface, you'd need StripeLoggingDecorator, PayPalLoggingDecorator, duplicating logic. The interface enables **runtime composition**: you can stack decorators in any order (logging wrapping caching wrapping validation) because each decorator accepts and returns the interface type—the chain assembles dynamically. It supports **testing**: you can inject a mock PaymentProcessor into a decorator to unit test the decorator's behavior without hitting real payment APIs.

Use interface-based decoration when you have **multiple implementations** of the same contract and want decorators that work with all of them, or when you want to **swap implementations** at runtime based on configuration.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Extending concrete class instead of interface**: Freshers create decorators that extend StripePaymentProcessor directly—this tight-couples the decorator to Stripe and breaks when you want to wrap PayPal or a test double. Always implement the interface.
- **Using concrete type for wrapped field**: Declaring wrapped as StripePaymentProcessor instead of PaymentProcessor means the decorator can only wrap that one implementation—use the interface type for the field so it accepts any conforming object.
- **Skipping the interface entirely**: Creating decorators without a shared contract means clients have to know whether they're calling the real component or a decorator—this breaks transparency and forces clients to depend on concrete types.
- **Not understanding Liskov Substitution**: Missing that the interface enables substitutability—decorators must honor the interface contract so they work anywhere the component works, which is the essence of the Liskov Substitution Principle.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Shared contract**: Component interface defines methods that both concrete components and decorators must implement, ensuring consistent behavior
- **Transparent wrapping**: Clients depend on interface type, not concrete classes—they can't tell if they're calling real component or decorated version
- **Substitutability**: Decorators are substitutable for components because they implement the same interface—this is Liskov Substitution Principle in action
- **Decorator reusability**: One decorator works with any component implementing the interface—no need for separate decorators per concrete class
- **Runtime composition**: Decorators accept and return interface type, enabling dynamic stacking in any order without compile-time dependencies
- **Interface type for wrapped field**: Wrapped component field should be declared as interface type, not concrete class, to accept any conforming implementation
- **Testing support**: Interface enables injecting mocks or stubs into decorators for unit testing without depending on real implementations

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The component interface is the shared contract that makes Decorator work. It defines the methods that both the real component and all decorators must implement. This ensures decorators can transparently wrap the component—clients interact with the interface and don't know whether they're calling the real object or a stack of decorators. Say you've got a PaymentProcessor interface with processPayment and refund methods. StripePaymentProcessor and PayPalPaymentProcessor both implement it. Now you write LoggingPaymentDecorator. It also implements PaymentProcessor, takes a PaymentProcessor in the constructor, and delegates to it after adding logging. The key is that the decorator holds the wrapped processor as an interface type, not a concrete class. That means you can wrap Stripe, PayPal, or even another decorator—they all implement the interface. Clients depend on PaymentProcessor, so they can use any of these interchangeably. That's substitutability. Decorators are substitutable for the component they wrap because they implement the same interface. This is the Liskov Substitution Principle: if you can use an object of type T, you should be able to use any object of a type that implements T without breaking anything. One mistake freshers make is creating decorators that extend the concrete class instead of implementing the interface. If LoggingPaymentDecorator extends StripePaymentProcessor, it's tightly coupled to Stripe. It won't work with PayPal, and you'll need separate decorators for every payment provider. Another mistake is declaring the wrapped field as a concrete type like StripePaymentProcessor. That breaks reusability. Always use the interface type for the wrapped field so it accepts any implementation. The interface is what enables transparent wrapping, runtime composition, and decorator reusability. Without it, the pattern doesn't work.

questions.question: What is the Decorator pattern and what problem does it solve?
questions.title: Decorator Pattern Explained
questions.direct_answer: The Decorator pattern wraps an object to add behavior dynamically without modifying its code. It solves the class explosion problem when you need multiple optional features that can combine in different ways—inheritance would require a subclass for every combination.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why composition beats inheritance when behaviors are optional and combinable.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Decorator is just another form of inheritance—missing that it wraps at runtime while inheritance is compile-time fixed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through a concrete scenario where inheritance causes exponential class growth and show how Decorator reduces it to linear growth.

sections.title: What Decorator Pattern Solves
sections.content:
The **Decorator pattern** addresses the problem of adding optional, combinable responsibilities to objects without creating an explosion of subclasses. Imagine a notification service that can send emails, which might need encryption, compression, or logging—any combination of these. With inheritance, you'd need classes like EncryptedNotifier, CompressedNotifier, EncryptedCompressedNotifier, LoggedEncryptedCompressedNotifier—the combinations grow exponentially. Decorator wraps the original object in layers, each adding one responsibility.

Think of it like wrapping a gift: the box is the core object, then you add layers of wrapping paper (encryption), ribbons (compression), and a card (logging)—each wrapper adds something without changing what's inside. The pattern follows the **Open/Closed Principle**: classes are open for extension (via wrapping) but closed for modification (the original class never changes).

sections.title: Decorator Pattern at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Component interface|~Shared contract|Notifier|all wrappers implement it|transparent stacking
blue|Concrete component|~Core object|EmailNotifier|does base behavior|gets wrapped
emerald|Decorator|~Wraps + delegates|holds inner ref|adds before/after|stack at runtime
violet|Why|~Avoid class explosion|N add-ons -> N classes|not 2^N subclasses|Open/Closed

sections.title: Decorator Pattern Implementation
When to Use Decorator
sections.content:
Use Decorator when you need **optional behaviors that can combine**: a discount system where orders might get holiday discounts, loyalty discounts, or bulk discounts in any combination—each decorator adds one discount type without knowing about others.

Use it for **cross-cutting concerns**: adding caching, logging, or monitoring to service methods without polluting business logic.

Use it when **inheritance creates exponential class growth**: if you have 3 optional features, inheritance needs 8 classes (2³), but Decorator needs only 4 (base + 3 decorators).

Use it when behaviors need to be **added or removed at runtime**: wrapping a repository with caching during high traffic, removing it during off-peak hours.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating it as inheritance**: Freshers think Decorator is just extending a class and don't realize it's about runtime wrapping—Decorator holds a reference to the wrapped object, inheritance creates a subtype hierarchy.
- **Forgetting to delegate**: Writing a decorator that adds behavior but forgets to call wrapped.method() means the original functionality is lost—the decorator must always delegate unless it's intentionally replacing behavior.
- **Skipping the interface**: Implementing decorators that extend the concrete class directly breaks substitutability—if EmailNotifier changes, every decorator breaks. The component interface ensures decorators work with any implementation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Wrapper composition**: Decorators wrap an object and implement the same interface, enabling transparent stacking of behaviors at runtime
- **Linear growth**: N optional features need N+1 classes (base + N decorators), while inheritance needs 2^N classes for all combinations
- **Open/Closed Principle**: Original class stays closed for modification, new decorators extend behavior without touching existing code
- **Runtime flexibility**: Behaviors can be added or removed by wrapping or unwrapping objects dynamically based on conditions
- **Component interface**: Shared contract ensures decorators are substitutable for the original object—client code can't tell the difference
- **Cross-cutting concerns**: Perfect for adding logging, caching, validation, or monitoring without coupling infrastructure to business logic
- **Delegation chain**: Each decorator delegates to wrapped object after adding behavior—the chain executes in wrapping order

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Decorator pattern wraps an object to add behavior without changing it. It solves the class explosion problem when you have optional features that can combine. Say you've got a notification service that sends emails. You might need to add encryption, compression, or logging—any combination. With inheritance, you'd need classes for every combo: encrypted, compressed, encrypted-and-compressed, logged-encrypted-compressed. That grows exponentially. With Decorator, you wrap the base notifier in layers. The encryption decorator wraps the base, the logging decorator wraps that, and so on. Each decorator implements the same interface, holds a reference to the wrapped object, and adds its behavior before or after delegating. Think of it like gift wrapping: the box is the core, then you add paper, ribbons, a card—each layer adds something without changing what's inside. I'd use this in a Spring Boot cart service for adding discount calculations. The base cart calculates totals, then you wrap it with holiday discount decorator, loyalty discount decorator, bulk discount decorator—they stack up at runtime. One mistake freshers make is thinking Decorator is just inheritance with a different name. It's not. Inheritance is compile-time and fixed. Decorator is runtime and flexible. You can swap decorators in and out based on conditions, which you can't do with subclasses.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Decorator solves a specific problem — class explosion — that inheritance creates when you have optional, combinable behaviors.

beats.content: Start with a Coffee class and five optional add-ons: milk, sugar, vanilla, cream, caramel. Using inheritance, each combination needs its own class. Five add-ons, thirty-two possible combinations, thirty-two classes. That's the explosion Decorator prevents.

Decorator wraps instead of extends. MilkDecorator wraps any Coffee, adds milk cost, appends to description, and delegates everything else to the wrapped object. SugarDecorator does the same. You compose at runtime: new SugarDecorator(new MilkDecorator(new SimpleCoffee())). Three small classes handle all combinations.

The canonical Java example is IO streams. new DataInputStream(new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(file))) stacks three decorators. Each adds one capability — buffering, type-aware reading — without knowing or caring what it wraps.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: All decorators must implement the same interface as the component they wrap. That's what makes them interchangeable. A decorator that extends the concrete class instead of the interface breaks composability.

questions.question: How do Java IO streams demonstrate the Decorator pattern?
questions.title: Java IO Streams as Decorator Pattern
questions.direct_answer: Java IO uses Decorator extensively: InputStream is the component interface, FileInputStream and ByteArrayInputStream are concrete components, and FilterInputStream is the base decorator. BufferedInputStream, DataInputStream, and others wrap streams to add buffering, typed reading, or compression without changing the underlying stream.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can identify design patterns in standard library code you've used—not just recognize them in academic examples.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Java IO as just a random collection of classes—missing that it's a deliberate Decorator implementation showing the pattern's power.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Sketch the wrapping chain for a real scenario: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(file))) and explain what each layer adds.

sections.title: Decorator Pattern in Java IO Streams
sections.content:
Java's IO library is a textbook implementation of the **Decorator pattern**. The **InputStream** class acts as the component interface (though it's abstract, not an interface). Concrete streams like **FileInputStream** (reads from files) and **ByteArrayInputStream** (reads from memory) are the base components. Then **FilterInputStream** serves as the abstract base decorator—it holds a reference to another InputStream and delegates all calls to it. Concrete decorators like **BufferedInputStream** (adds buffering), **DataInputStream** (adds typed reading like readInt()), and **GZIPInputStream** (adds decompression) extend FilterInputStream. Each adds one responsibility without changing the underlying stream.

Think of it like a water pipe system: FileInputStream is the source pipe, BufferedInputStream is a pipe that adds a water tank for smoother flow, DataInputStream is a pipe with a meter that reads specific measurements—you connect them in any order based on what you need.

sections.title: Java IO as Decorator at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|InputStream|~Component (abstract)|the shared type|read() contract|base of the hierarchy
blue|FileInputStream|~Concrete component|raw bytes from file|the real source|gets wrapped
emerald|FilterInputStream|~Base decorator|holds an InputStream|delegates all calls|extend to add behavior
violet|Buffered / Data / GZIP|~Concrete decorators|buffering|typed reads|decompression - stack freely

sections.title: Java IO Decorator Chain Example
When Java IO Decorators Shine
sections.content:
Use **BufferedInputStream** when reading many small chunks from a file or network socket—it reduces system calls by reading in blocks and serving from an internal buffer, boosting performance 10-100x.

Use **DataInputStream** when reading binary files with structured data like integers or doubles—it handles byte-to-type conversion so you don't manually reconstruct ints from four bytes.

Use **GZIPInputStream** when reading compressed files—it transparently decompresses while you read normally. Combine them for complex scenarios: reading a gzipped binary file needs new DataInputStream(new GZIPInputStream(new FileInputStream(file)))—each decorator adds one capability. The pattern lets Java provide a small core of stream types and many optional decorators that combine freely, instead of having classes like BufferedFileDataStream for every combination.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not closing the outermost stream**: Freshers close the FileInputStream directly, thinking they need to close each layer—but closing the outermost decorator (like DataInputStream) automatically closes the entire chain, and closing inner streams first can cause issues.
- **Wrapping in wrong order**: Wrapping BufferedInputStream inside DataInputStream instead of outside—the buffering layer should be closest to the raw source so DataInputStream reads from the buffer, not from disk repeatedly.
- **Not recognizing the pattern**: Treating Java IO as random classes with weird nesting syntax—missing that it's Decorator in action helps you understand why the API is designed this way and how to build custom stream decorators when needed.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **InputStream hierarchy**: InputStream is the component interface, FileInputStream and ByteArrayInputStream are concrete components, FilterInputStream is base decorator
- **FilterInputStream**: Abstract decorator that holds wrapped stream and delegates all methods—concrete decorators extend it and override only methods they enhance
- **BufferedInputStream**: Adds buffering by reading chunks into memory—reduces disk/network access from thousands of one-byte reads to dozens of block reads
- **DataInputStream**: Adds typed reading methods like readInt() and readDouble()—handles byte-to-primitive conversion so you don't manually parse binary data
- **Wrapping chain**: Decorators nest via constructor: new DataInputStream(new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(file))) builds the stack
- **Close propagation**: Closing the outermost decorator closes the entire chain—no need to close each layer individually
- **Flexible composition**: Java provides ~10 stream types and ~15 decorators that combine freely instead of 150+ specialized classes for every combination

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Java IO is built on Decorator pattern. InputStream is the component interface—well, it's an abstract class, but it plays that role. Concrete streams like FileInputStream and ByteArrayInputStream are the base components. They just read raw bytes from a source. Then FilterInputStream is the base decorator—it wraps another stream and delegates everything to it. Concrete decorators like BufferedInputStream, DataInputStream, and GZIPInputStream extend FilterInputStream and add specific behaviors. BufferedInputStream adds buffering so you're not hitting disk on every single byte read. DataInputStream adds typed reading—methods like readInt or readDouble that handle the byte-to-number conversion for you. GZIPInputStream adds decompression. You stack them by nesting constructors: new BufferedReader, wrapping InputStreamReader, wrapping FileInputStream. Each layer adds one capability. The file stream reads raw bytes, the input stream reader converts bytes to characters, the buffered reader adds buffering and line-by-line reading. That's Decorator in action. One common mistake is not realizing this is a pattern. Freshers see the weird nested syntax and think it's just quirky API design. But it's deliberate—Decorator lets Java provide a small set of base streams and decorators that combine flexibly instead of having a giant class for every possible combination. Another mistake is closing streams in the wrong order or closing each layer separately. You only close the outermost decorator, and it closes the entire chain automatically.

DataInputStream — wraps any InputStream and adds readInt(), readDouble(), readUTF()

beats.content: Composed: new DataInputStream(new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream('data.bin'))). Each decorator is unaware of what it wraps — it only knows the InputStream interface. Adding a new stream capability means a new FilterInputStream subclass, zero changes to anything else.

questions.question: How do you use Decorator to add logging or caching to a service without changing it?
questions.title: Decorator for Logging and Caching in Services
questions.direct_answer: Create decorator classes that implement the same service interface, wrap the original service instance, and add logging or caching before or after delegating to the wrapped service. This keeps cross-cutting concerns separate from business logic and follows the Open/Closed Principle.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can apply Decorator to real backend services—not just toy examples with coffee or shapes.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding logging directly inside the service method—this couples infrastructure concerns to business logic and violates Single Responsibility Principle.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect Decorator to Spring's proxy-based features: at-Cacheable and at-Transactional are Decorator implementations via dynamic proxies—explain how Spring wraps your service at runtime.

sections.title: Decorator for Cross-Cutting Concerns
sections.content:
In a Spring Boot backend, you often need to add **cross-cutting concerns** like logging, caching, or metrics to services without polluting business logic. The Decorator pattern solves this by wrapping the service with decorator classes that add these concerns. Each decorator implements the same **service interface**, holds a reference to the wrapped service, and adds behavior before or after delegating method calls. For example, a **LoggingOrderService** wraps the real OrderService, logs method entry and exit with parameters and timing, then delegates to the wrapped service. A **CachingOrderService** checks a cache Map before delegating, stores results after successful calls.

Think of it like airport security layers: your luggage (the request) goes through scanner A (logging decorator), then scanner B (caching decorator), then finally reaches the inspection agent (real service)—each layer adds a check without changing what the agent does. This keeps **business logic pure** and makes decorators reusable across different services.

sections.title: Service Decorators at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Service interface|~OrderService|real + decorators implement|substitutable|business logic stays pure
blue|LoggingDecorator|~Cross-cutting|log entry/exit + timing|delegate to wrapped|reusable across services
emerald|CachingDecorator|~Cross-cutting|check cache first|store after delegate|evict on write
violet|Spring link|~@Cacheable / @Transactional|dynamic proxy = decorator|wraps your bean|self-calls bypass it

sections.title: Service Decorator with Logging and Caching
When to Use Service Decorators
sections.content:
Use decorators for **debugging in development**: wrap services with LoggingDecorator to trace all method calls and parameters without changing production code—remove the decorator in production by changing one configuration line.

Use for **performance optimization**: wrap expensive services with CachingDecorator or RateLimitingDecorator to add caching or throttling without modifying the service implementation.

Use for **monitoring and metrics**: wrap services with MetricsDecorator that records call counts, response times, and error rates—this keeps instrumentation separate from business logic.

Use when **multiple concerns need to combine**: a payment service might need logging, caching, and retry logic—stack three decorators instead of creating a PaymentServiceWithLoggingCachingAndRetry class. In Spring, this pattern is automated: at-Cacheable and at-Transactional use dynamic proxies to wrap your beans, which is Decorator under the hood.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding concerns directly in service**: Freshers put logging statements inside business methods, mixing infrastructure with domain logic—this violates Single Responsibility Principle and makes the service harder to test and maintain.
- **Forgetting to implement the interface**: Creating a decorator that extends the concrete class instead of implementing the interface breaks substitutability and couples the decorator to one implementation.
- **Not delegating all methods**: Implementing only the decorated methods and forgetting others causes runtime errors when clients call unimplemented methods—use an abstract base decorator that delegates everything by default.
- **Overusing decorators**: Adding decorators for every tiny concern creates deep wrapping chains that are hard to debug—sometimes a simple method call or aspect-oriented programming is cleaner.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cross-cutting concerns**: Decorator separates logging, caching, metrics, and validation from business logic, keeping services focused on domain behavior
- **Interface implementation**: Decorators must implement the same interface as the service they wrap to maintain substitutability and type safety
- **Delegation mechanics**: Decorator adds behavior before or after delegating to wrapped service—never replaces the original behavior unless that's the intent
- **Runtime composition**: Stack decorators in any order based on configuration—logging outside caching means you log cache hits, caching outside logging means you cache logged results
- **Spring connection**: at-Cacheable and at-Transactional use dynamic proxies to wrap beans—Spring generates decorator classes at runtime that add caching or transaction management
- **Testability**: Decorators are easy to unit test—inject a mock wrapped service and verify the decorator adds behavior correctly without hitting real dependencies
- **Reusability**: One LoggingDecorator works with any service interface—no need to write logging code in every service class

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You use Decorator to add logging or caching without changing the service by wrapping it. Create a decorator class that implements the same service interface, takes the real service as a constructor parameter, and adds behavior before or after delegating. For example, a LoggingOrderService implements OrderService, wraps the real OrderService, and logs method calls and execution time before delegating. A CachingOrderService checks a cache Map before calling the wrapped service, and stores results after. You can stack them: wrap the real service with caching, then wrap that with logging. Now every call goes through logging, then caching, then the real service. This keeps cross-cutting concerns separate from business logic—the real OrderService doesn't know it's being logged or cached. It follows the Open-Closed Principle: you extend behavior without modifying existing code. In Spring, this pattern is automated. When you use at-Cacheable on a service method, Spring wraps your bean in a dynamic proxy at runtime—the proxy is a decorator that checks the cache before calling your method. Same with at-Transactional: Spring wraps your service in a decorator that starts a transaction, calls your method, then commits or rolls back. One mistake freshers make is adding logging directly inside the service method. That couples infrastructure to business logic and makes testing harder. Another is not implementing the interface—if your decorator extends the concrete class, it's tightly coupled and won't work with different implementations.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Decorator is the pattern behind @Cacheable and @Transactional — understanding it explains why those annotations have the limitations they do.

beats.content: For a ProductService interface, you can add logging and caching without touching the real service at all. LoggingProductService implements the same interface, wraps the real service, logs before and after, and delegates. CachingProductService wraps that and checks the cache first.
Composition: new LoggingProductService(new CachingProductService(new RealProductService())). Calls flow through logging, then caching, then the real service. Each layer is testable independently.

Spring does this automatically via AOP proxies. When you add @Transactional, Spring generates a proxy decorator around your bean. The proxy wraps your method call in transaction setup and teardown. You never write the decorator — Spring generates it at startup.

speakable_v2.cap: production trap: @Transactional doesn't work on self-calls because the proxy is bypassed. When a method inside a Spring bean calls another method on the same object, the call goes directly to the real object, not through the proxy decorator — so no transaction boundary is created.

questions.question: When should you use Decorator pattern instead of inheritance?
questions.title: Decorator vs Inheritance: When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: Use Decorator when you need optional, combinable behaviors at runtime or when inheritance would cause class explosion. Use inheritance when the relationship is a stable is-a with fixed behavior and you're modeling true type hierarchy, not adding responsibilities.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you have a decision principle for choosing composition versus inheritance—not just memorizing that composition is always better.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using inheritance for every extension need—leads to deep, brittle hierarchies that can't adapt when requirements change.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through a specific scenario where inheritance creates exponential class growth, then show how Decorator reduces it to linear growth with concrete numbers.

sections.title: Decorator vs Inheritance Decision Framework
sections.content:
Choosing between Decorator and inheritance comes down to whether you're modeling **type relationships** or **adding responsibilities**. Inheritance is for **is-a relationships**: a SavingsAccount is-a BankAccount, a Manager is-an Employee—these are stable type hierarchies where subclasses specialize the parent. Decorator is for **adding optional behaviors**: taking an Order and adding gift-wrapping, expedited shipping, or insurance—these are responsibilities that can combine in any way and change at runtime. Inheritance locks in behavior at compile time: once you create ExpressShippingOrder as a subclass, every instance has express shipping permanently. Decorator wraps at runtime: you decide per-order whether to wrap it with ExpressShippingDecorator.

The key question: **do you have N optional features that can combine?** Inheritance needs 2^N classes for all combinations; Decorator needs N+1 classes (base + N decorators). For 3 features: inheritance needs 8 classes, Decorator needs 4.

sections.title: Inheritance vs Decorator at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Inheritance|~is-a, compile-time|stable type hierarchy|fixed at creation|2^N for combos
blue|Decorator|~has-a, runtime|optional responsibilities|add/remove dynamically|N+1 for combos
emerald|The math|~Class count|3 features = 8 vs 4|5 features = 32 vs 6|linear beats exponential
violet|Choose|~Model vs add-on|Car is-a Vehicle -> extend|Order + giftwrap -> decorate|combos -> decorate

sections.title: Inheritance Explosion vs Decorator in Code
Step 1: Count Combinations
sections.content: Start by counting how many optional features you have and whether they can combine. If you have **shipping options** (standard, express, overnight) and **packaging options** (regular, gift-wrap), that's 2 dimensions that can combine: standard with regular, standard with gift-wrap, express with regular, and so on. Inheritance needs ShippingOrder, ExpressShippingOrder, GiftWrapOrder, ExpressGiftWrapOrder, OvernightOrder, OvernightGiftWrapOrder—6 classes and growing. Decorator needs Order (base), ExpressShippingDecorator, OvernightShippingDecorator, GiftWrapDecorator—4 classes total. As you add features (insurance, tracking), inheritance grows exponentially, Decorator grows linearly. If combinations are rare or you have only 1-2 non-combining features, inheritance might be simpler.

sections.title: Step 2: Assess Runtime Flexibility Needs
sections.content: Ask whether behaviors need to change at runtime based on user choices or conditions. If a customer can toggle gift-wrapping on and off in the cart, or if you enable express shipping during checkout based on delivery address, you need **runtime composition**—Decorator handles this naturally by wrapping or unwrapping objects. Inheritance is static: once you instantiate GiftWrapOrder, you can't remove the gift-wrapping without creating a new instance. If behaviors are fixed for the lifetime of the object and determined at creation time—like a Car that's either Electric or Gasoline, never switching—inheritance is appropriate. Decorator adds complexity if you don't need runtime flexibility, so don't use it just because composition is fashionable.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using inheritance for optional features**: Freshers create subclasses like OrderWithLogging, OrderWithCaching, OrderWithLoggingAndCaching—this creates exponential class growth and makes it impossible to add combinations not anticipated upfront.
- **Using Decorator for type hierarchies**: Creating VehicleDecorator to wrap Car, Truck, Motorcycle misses that these are distinct types with different contracts—inheritance is correct here because they model an is-a relationship, not optional behaviors.
- **Overcomplicating simple cases**: If you only have one or two features that don't combine and are fixed at creation, inheritance is cleaner—Decorator adds wrapping boilerplate without benefit.
- **Ignoring the Open-Closed Principle**: Using inheritance for every extension means modifying the class hierarchy when requirements change—Decorator lets you add new decorators without touching existing code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Class count math**: N optional combinable features need 2^N classes with inheritance but only N+1 classes with Decorator
- **Is-a vs has-behavior**: Use inheritance for stable type relationships (Car is-a Vehicle), Decorator for optional responsibilities (Order has express-shipping)
- **Runtime vs compile-time**: Decorator composes behaviors at runtime based on conditions; inheritance fixes them at compile time when you write subclasses
- **Open-Closed Principle**: Decorator extends behavior without modifying existing classes; inheritance requires changing the hierarchy when adding features
- **Liskov Substitution**: Both must respect substitutability—decorators must work anywhere the base object works, subclasses must honor parent contracts
- **Complexity trade-off**: Decorator adds wrapping complexity; inheritance adds class count complexity—choose based on which grows faster with requirements
- **Real example**: Java IO uses Decorator because streams have optional features (buffering, compression) that combine; Collections framework uses inheritance because List, Set, Map are distinct types

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Use Decorator when you need optional behaviors that can combine in different ways, or when inheritance would create too many classes. Use inheritance when you're modeling a true type hierarchy with a stable is-a relationship. Here's the key difference: inheritance is compile-time and fixed, Decorator is runtime and flexible. Say you've got a notification system. You might send notifications by email, SMS, or push. Those are the base types—that's inheritance. But each notification might need encryption, compression, or logging—those are optional and can combine. With inheritance, you'd need EncryptedEmailNotifier, CompressedEmailNotifier, EncryptedCompressedEmailNotifier, plus all the SMS and push variants. That's exponential growth: three base types times eight combinations equals twenty-four classes. With Decorator, you have three base types plus three decorators—six classes total. You wrap notifications at runtime based on what each user needs. The math matters. If you have N optional features that can combine, inheritance needs 2 to the N classes. Decorator needs N plus one. For three features, that's eight versus four. For five features, it's thirty-two versus six. Decorator scales linearly; inheritance scales exponentially. One mistake freshers make is using inheritance for everything because it's simpler upfront. But when requirements change and you need new combinations, you're stuck adding more subclasses. Decorator keeps your classes open for extension but closed for modification—you add new decorators without touching existing code.

questions.question: How do you implement a simple Decorator pattern in Java?
questions.title: Implementing Decorator Pattern in Java
questions.direct_answer: Define a component interface, create a concrete implementation, then build decorator classes that implement the interface, wrap a component instance via constructor injection, and add behavior before or after delegating to the wrapped object. An abstract base decorator handles the delegation boilerplate.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can code the Decorator pattern from scratch—not just describe it—and understand the delegation mechanics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to implement the same interface in the decorator—breaks the substitutability that makes Decorator work.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Add an abstract BaseDecorator class that holds the wrapped component and delegates by default—concrete decorators only override methods where they add behavior.

sections.title: Decorator Pattern Implementation Structure
sections.content:
Implementing Decorator in Java involves four core elements: the **component interface** that defines the contract, a **concrete component** that implements the base behavior, an **abstract base decorator** that implements the interface and holds a reference to another component, and **concrete decorators** that extend the base decorator and override methods to add behavior. The abstract decorator handles delegation boilerplate—it implements all interface methods by forwarding to the wrapped component, so concrete decorators only override methods where they add something.

Think of it like a relay race: the interface defines the race contract (run 100 meters), the concrete component is the first runner, the base decorator is the baton-passing mechanism, and concrete decorators are relay stations that do something (take measurement, record time) before passing the baton. The pattern requires **constructor injection** of the wrapped component and **delegation** after adding behavior—these two mechanics are what make Decorator work.

sections.title: Four-Layer Decorator Structure
sections.content:
amber|1. Interface|~Coffee|cost(), description()|the contract|enables substitutability
blue|2. Concrete component|~SimpleCoffee|base behavior|the thing wrapped|implements interface
emerald|3. Base decorator|~abstract CoffeeDecorator|holds wrapped (protected)|delegates by default|cuts boilerplate
violet|4. Concrete decorators|~Milk, Sugar|override + delegate|super(coffee)|compose by nesting

sections.title: Complete Decorator Implementation
When This Implementation Approach Works
sections.content:
Use the **abstract base decorator** pattern when your interface has multiple methods and you want concrete decorators to only override the ones they enhance—the base decorator provides default delegation for everything else, reducing boilerplate.

Use **constructor injection** for the wrapped component when the decorator needs it for its entire lifetime—this is the standard approach because decorators always need to delegate.

Use method-level composition (passing the component to a method instead of constructor) only if the decorator is stateless and wrapping is per-call, which is rare. This implementation works for **any domain**: payment processing (add fraud check, logging decorators), data access (add caching, retry decorators), or UI components (add border, scroll decorators in GUI frameworks). The four-layer structure is the blueprint—adjust names and methods to your domain but keep the structure intact.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Skipping the base decorator**: Freshers make each concrete decorator implement the interface directly, duplicating delegation code in every decorator—the abstract base decorator exists to eliminate this duplication by delegating once.
- **Decorator not implementing interface**: Creating a decorator that extends the concrete component instead of implementing the interface breaks substitutability—clients can't treat decorated and undecorated objects uniformly.
- **Forgetting to call wrapped method**: Adding behavior in a decorator but not delegating to the wrapped object means the original functionality is lost—always delegate unless you're intentionally replacing behavior.
- **Exposing wrapped field**: Making the wrapped field public or giving it a getter breaks encapsulation—clients shouldn't know or care that they're talking to a decorator, and accessing the wrapped object directly bypasses decorator behavior.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four-layer structure**: Component interface → Concrete component → Abstract base decorator → Concrete decorators
- **Constructor injection**: Wrapped component is passed to decorator constructor and stored in a final field—ensures decorator has it for entire lifetime
- **Abstract base decorator**: Implements interface and delegates all methods to wrapped component by default—concrete decorators only override methods they enhance
- **Override and delegate**: Concrete decorators override methods, add behavior before or after, then call wrapped.method() to preserve original functionality
- **Interface substitutability**: Decorators implement the same interface as the component they wrap—clients can't distinguish decorated from undecorated objects
- **Protected wrapped field**: Base decorator stores wrapped component as protected so concrete decorators can access it for delegation
- **Composition over inheritance**: Decorator uses composition (has-a wrapped component) instead of inheritance (is-a subtype) to add behavior flexibly

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To implement Decorator in Java, you need four pieces. First, define a component interface with the methods you want to decorate. Say it's Coffee with cost and description methods. Second, create a concrete component that implements the interface—SimpleCoffee implements those methods with base behavior. Third, make an abstract base decorator that also implements the interface. It holds a reference to another Coffee in a protected field, takes it via constructor, and delegates all methods to it by default. Fourth, create concrete decorators that extend the base decorator and override only the methods where they add behavior. So MilkDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator, overrides cost to add point-five dollars, and overrides description to append comma-milk. Same with SugarDecorator. Each concrete decorator calls the wrapped method after adding behavior—that's the delegation chain. To use it, you nest constructors: new SugarDecorator wrapping new MilkDecorator wrapping new SimpleCoffee. When you call cost on the outermost decorator, it adds its cost, then calls wrapped-dot-cost, which adds its cost, then calls wrapped-dot-cost, which returns the base cost. The whole chain executes. The key parts are: the interface for substitutability, the base decorator for delegation boilerplate, and constructor injection of the wrapped component. One mistake is skipping the base decorator and duplicating delegation in every concrete decorator. Another is not implementing the interface—if your decorator extends SimpleCoffee directly, it's tightly coupled to that one implementation and won't work with other Coffee types.
